lesson.title: Exactly One Answer: Independent Systems
lesson.summary: An independent system is a consistent system whose lines cross at exactly one point, giving a single unique solution rather than none or infinitely many.
lesson.body:
A consistent system, recall, is one with at least one solution. An independent system narrows that down further: it is a consistent system with exactly one solution, no more and no less. That single ordered pair is the only point that lies on both lines, which makes it the most common and most useful case in practical problems, since it usually points to one specific, meaningful answer rather than a range of possibilities or an empty set. In a real-world setting, such as finding the price and quantity that satisfy two different cost equations, that single answer is often exactly what the problem is asking for.

Geometrically, an independent system corresponds to two distinct lines with different slopes. Two lines with different slopes are guaranteed to cross at exactly one point somewhere on the plane, no matter what their y-intercepts happen to be, which is why checking the slopes is often the fastest way to predict that a system will be independent before doing any further algebra. This is a useful shortcut for classifying a system quickly, even before solving it completely, and it works because two lines with different rates of change can only stay the same distance apart, or cross, and never both at once.

Consider the system 3x - 2y = 4 and x + y = 3. Solve the second equation for y: y = 3 - x. Substitute this expression into the first equation: 3x - 2(3 - x) = 4. Distributing the -2 gives 3x - 6 + 2x = 4, which combines to 5x - 6 = 4, so 5x = 10, and x = 2. Substituting back, y = 3 - 2 = 1. Check both originals: 3(2) - 2(1) = 6 - 2 = 4 matches the first equation, and 2 + 1 = 3 matches the second. The ordered pair (2, 1) is confirmed as a solution, and because it is the only pair that satisfies both equations, it is the unique solution of this system.

To see why this is the only solution, compare the slopes. Rewriting 3x - 2y = 4 as y = (3/2)x - 2 shows a slope of 3/2. Rewriting x + y = 3 as y = -x + 3 shows a slope of -1. Since 3/2 does not equal -1, the two lines are guaranteed to intersect at exactly one point, and that point is the (2, 1) found above, confirming both that a solution exists and that it is unique, matching the definition of an independent system exactly.

The name independent reflects the fact that neither equation can be produced from the other by simple scaling; each contributes genuinely separate information that narrows the solution set down to one point. This is why most systems built from real situations, like combining cost and quantity constraints, come out independent: two unrelated pieces of information about the same two unknowns typically pin down exactly one answer, in contrast with the dependent systems explored in the next section, where the two equations turn out to carry the same information in disguise. Recognizing that contrast in advance, simply by comparing slopes, can save a great deal of unnecessary algebra.
